about: Lines marked with a quote are Bobby Fischer's own words, with their source. Everything else was written for the bot and is not a quotation. A line with "since" refers to something that had not happened before that year.

start_as_white.text: I have White. That's usually enough.
First move is mine. I don't waste it.
White. You'll be defending for a while.
I open, you answer. That's the arrangement.
With White I ask the questions.
My move. First the center, then your king.
Anything less than a full point with White is a bad day.
I'm White. Have a defense ready.
I'm not here to split the point.
I decided on my first move a long time ago.
You get Black. Somebody has to.

start_as_black.text: You have White. Make it count.
Your move. I've seen most of them.
King's pawn or queen's pawn? I have an answer for both.
The first move is yours. The initiative won't be for long.
Go ahead. Open with whatever you like.
White moves first. That's all White gets.
Black is fine. I've won plenty of games from this side.
Play your opening. I've prepared for it.
White is yours. So is the first mistake.
I have Black. Don't mistake that for defending.
Start whenever you like. I'm already thinking.
You open. I'll take it from there.

level_1956.text: I'm thirteen. The pieces don't care how old I am.
Thirteen years old, and I play every game to win.
Take me lightly if you want. It's been tried.
I've been at this since I was six. Seven years is a long time.
1956. U.S. Junior Champion, and just getting started.
This is the year I let Donald Byrne take my queen.
You'll get mistakes from me at this age. Don't count on them.
I improve every week. You're catching me early.

level_1958.text: Fifteen, and a grandmaster. Nobody has done it younger.
Portorož made me a grandmaster. I'm fifteen.
U.S. Champion at fourteen. Grandmaster at fifteen. I'm in a hurry.
I'm fifteen and already a Candidate for the world title.
The youngest grandmaster there is. Judge the moves, not the age.
At fifteen I'm playing the best in the world. Today I play you.
I'm fifteen. I've stopped being surprised when I win.
Portorož was my first Interzonal. It won't be my last.

level_1963.text: Eleven games, eleven wins. That was my U.S. Championship.
U.S. Champion. Eleven opponents, and not one draw.
Eleven straight wins. I'm not in a generous mood.
Nobody took half a point from me at the U.S. Championship. You may try.
You picked the year I won eleven out of eleven. Good luck.
A perfect score at the U.S. Championship. I see no reason to stop there.
Twenty years old and U.S. Champion again. It's becoming a habit.

level_1972.text: World Champion. I hope you came prepared.
Taimanov, Larsen, Petrosian, Spassky. Now you.
Reykjavik, 1972. This is the player Spassky had to face.
You chose the World Champion. I respect the nerve.
This is my best chess. Don't expect gifts.
I took the title from Spassky. Let's see what you can do.
The title doesn't make the moves. I do.
I prepared for Spassky for years. For you, I'll improvise.

book_move.text: I played this at {event}, {year}. It was right then and it's right now.
{opponent} had to answer this at {event}. Now you do.
Nothing new. I played it against {opponent} at {event}.
{opponent} sat where you are. That was {event}, {year}.
Straight from {event}, {year}. {opponent} was across the board.
I don't guess in the opening. This is from {event}, {year}.
My move against {opponent} at {event}. I see no reason to change it.

book_move_1972.text: Reykjavik, game {game}. I played this against Spassky.
Game {game} of the match. Same move.
I played it in game {game} against Spassky. I'll play it against you.
You're getting what Spassky got in game {game}.
Game {game}, Reykjavik. I don't forget those.
This was good enough for the title match. Game {game}.
The whole chess world watched me play this. Game {game}.
Game {game} against Spassky went this way. I know the road.
In game {game} Spassky had your pieces.
From the match with Spassky. Game {game}, 1972.

book_move_memorable.text: I put this game in my book. {opponent}, {year}.
{opponent}, {year}. One of the sixty I chose to annotate.
This move is in my book. The game with {opponent}.
{opponent}, {year}. That game is in my book for a reason.
A memorable game. {opponent} had your side in {year}.
You can look this up. My game with {opponent}, {year}.
I wrote the notes to this game myself. {opponent}, {year}.
Sixty games made my book. This is from the one with {opponent}.
{year}, against {opponent}. I thought it worth writing about.
I know this game by heart. I annotated it. {opponent}, {year}.
Against {opponent} in {year} I played this. It made the book.

player_follows_history.text: Same as {opponent} in {year}. I know what comes next.
{opponent} chose that against me. Go on.
My game with {opponent} went the same way. {year}.
So you play it like {opponent}. We'll see for how long.
{opponent}'s choice in {year}. I had a reply ready then, too.
You and {opponent} had the same thought. {year}.
Exactly what {opponent} did. I remember my answer.

player_leaves_history.text: {opponent} played {san} here. You're on your own now.
{opponent} chose {san}. You have your own ideas.
Here {opponent} played {san}. Let's see if yours is better.
You've left my game with {opponent}. It went {san}.
That isn't how {opponent} played it. The move there was {san}.
{opponent} went {san}. Now we both have to think.
So much for following {opponent}. That game continued {san}.
We part company with {opponent} here. I was expecting {san}.
Hm. {opponent} didn't try that. It was {san}, as I recall.

out_of_book.text: From here it's over the board.
No more memory. Just the position.
Now we find out who understands the position.
Nothing to remember now. Only moves to find.
On my own from here. So are you.
I'm done reciting. Now I calculate.
My preparation ends here. My chess doesn't.
This is where the game really starts.
This move I had to find myself.
Good. I prefer thinking to remembering.

opening_sicilian_najdorf.text: The Najdorf. I know every corner of it.
Najdorf Sicilian. I've lived in these positions since I was a boy.
The Najdorf. Sharp and sound. That's why I play it.
The Najdorf. One loose move here and it's over.
A Najdorf. I've taken a poisoned pawn or two in this opening.
The Najdorf. Nobody gets a quiet game out of it.

opening_sicilian.text: The Sicilian. I've spent more hours on it than on anything else.
A Sicilian. Nobody plays it to make a draw.
Sicilian Defense. Unbalanced from the first move, which suits me.
A wing pawn for a center pawn. That's the whole Sicilian bargain.
Good, a Sicilian. I've won with it and against it.
The Sicilian. One slow move and the other side's attack arrives first.
The Sicilian. My bishop on c4 has beaten a good many of them.

opening_ruy_lopez.text: The Ruy Lopez. Slow pressure, and it never lets up.
Ruy Lopez. I've won more games with it than I can count.
The Ruy Lopez. Black needs patience and exact moves.
The Ruy. I never get tired of it.
The Ruy Lopez. Four hundred years old, and still not solved.
Ruy Lopez. Spassky defended it against me in Reykjavik.
Ruy Lopez. Waste one tempo in this and you feel it for forty moves.

opening_kings_indian.text: The King's Indian. You can have the center. For now.
King's Indian. My bishop on g7 will have its say.
The King's Indian. I've trusted it my whole career.
King's Indian. White gets the space and I get the chances.
The King's Indian. Black gives ground early and collects later.
A King's Indian. Now nobody at this board is playing safe.
The King's Indian. Cramped at first. Then it uncoils.

opening_grunfeld.text: The Grünfeld. White builds a big center and I shoot at it.
Grünfeld Defense. Let White have the pawns. I'll have the targets.
The Grünfeld. Good enough for my game with Botvinnik. Good enough for this.
Grünfeld. Open lines for my pieces from the start. I like that.
The Grünfeld. Everything I have is aimed at d4.
A Grünfeld. Some of my best games started this way.
The Grünfeld. Sharp theory, and I know my way through it.

opening_french.text: The French. Black locks in a bishop on move one. I never saw the appeal.
French Defense. Solid, cramped, and I get the space.
The French. I've never trusted it for Black.
The French. Black bets everything on one pawn chain. I'll be hitting it.
The French. You get a wall of pawns and I get room to attack.
The French. The Winawer, if that's where we're headed, never convinced me.
The French has given me trouble before. I've done my homework.

opening_caro_kann.text: The Caro-Kann. Solid, and it dares White to get impatient.
Caro-Kann. Nothing to attack yet. I can wait.
The Caro-Kann. Petrosian played it against me more than once.
The Caro-Kann is a hard nut. I've cracked it before.
The Caro-Kann. Black gives nothing away and asks for very little.
A Caro-Kann. Sound enough, and it doesn't frighten anybody.
The Caro-Kann. Black wants a safe position. I want more than that.

opening_kings_gambit.text: I once wrote an article about the King's Gambit. It wasn't kind.
The King's Gambit: a pawn for an attack. Sometimes the attack shows up.
The King's Gambit. I've been on both sides of it.
Spassky beat me with the King's Gambit once. Then I went home and analyzed.
I called the King's Gambit unsound in print. I play it anyway.
In the King's Gambit Black can take the pawn. Keeping it is the whole argument.
The King's Gambit. Long out of fashion, and still dangerous.

opening_queens_gambit.text: The Queen's Gambit. Quiet on the surface. Don't believe it.
Queen's Gambit. Slow maneuvering. I can do that too.
A Queen's Gambit. Classical chess, the kind Capablanca played.
The Queen's Gambit. Small advantages, nursed for a long time.
Queen's Gambit. Spassky and I had this in Reykjavik.
The Queen's Gambit isn't my usual ground. I know it anyway.
The Queen's Gambit is all pawn structure. Mind yours.

opening_nimzo_indian.text: The Nimzo-Indian. I pin the knight and fight for e4.
Nimzo-Indian. Take the two bishops if you like. They won't come free.
The Nimzo-Indian. Solid, with plenty of bite.
Nimzo-Indian. I played it against Spassky in Reykjavik.
The Nimzo-Indian. If your pawns get doubled, I know where to aim.
Nimzo-Indian Defense. I haven't committed my center yet. You have.
The Nimzo-Indian. My bishop for your knight, if the price is right.

opening_english.text: The English. Quiet first moves, and the fight comes later.
English Opening. The c-pawn first. The center can wait.
The English. It can turn into almost anything.
English. I've played it and I've faced it. No surprises.
The English. Slow, with a sting in it.
English Opening. It's a fight for d5, whatever else it looks like.
The English. I opened with it myself in Reykjavik.

opening_alekhine.text: Alekhine's Defense. One knight invites the whole center forward.
Alekhine's Defense. White gets a lot of space. Maybe too much.
Alekhine's. I used it against Spassky in Reykjavik.
Alekhine's Defense. Those advanced pawns are strong or weak. We'll find out which.
Alekhine's Defense. Not many trust it. I've made it work.
Alekhine's Defense. Risky but playable. I like that kind.
Alekhine's. The pawns chase the knight now. The bill comes later.

opening_pirc_modern.text: The Pirc. Black hands White the center and means to take it back.
A Pirc setup. I tried it myself in Reykjavik.
The bishop on g7 waits. Everything else is still to be decided.
A free hand in the center for White. The question is what it's worth.
A counterpuncher's defense. Let White come forward, then hit back.
Nothing is in contact yet. That won't last.
This defense used to be called irregular. It's respectable now.

opening_italian.text: The Italian game. Old as the hills and still full of tricks.
The bishop on c4 is how Morphy played. I don't argue with Morphy.
The old Italian lines. Develop fast or get mated.
The old masters knew these positions. I studied the old masters.
The Italian. Everybody learns it first. Few learn it properly.
Old-fashioned chess. I happen to like old-fashioned chess.
In these lines a pawn matters less than a tempo.

opening_scandinavian.text: The Center Counter. I develop and you lose time. Simple.
Center Counter Defense. Black opens the center before developing a piece.
The Scandinavian. If the queen comes out early, I gain time chasing it.
The Center Counter. I've never lost sleep over it.
Center Counter. Some call it the Scandinavian. Either way White is better.
The Scandinavian. The center is settled on move one. That makes my job easier.
The Center Counter. Rare in grandmaster play. There are reasons.

opening_other_e4.text: Not the Sicilian, not the Ruy Lopez. Fine, I'll just play chess.
A king's pawn game with open lines. My kind of position.
Off the main roads. Good. I don't need a map.
You've stayed out of my main lines. That won't be enough.
King's pawn openings reward fast development. I develop fast.
I don't see this one often. I know what to do with it.
Whatever you answer the king's pawn with, I've looked at it.

opening_other_d4.text: A closed opening. The play is slower. The mistakes cost the same.
Queen's pawn games turn on one pawn break. I know which one I want.
The queen's pawn. I've spent years taking these positions apart.
Queen's pawn. This will be about squares, not tricks.
A queen's pawn game off the usual track. I'll find my own way.
Queen's pawn. No hurry. I can outsit anybody.
Queen's pawn. I don't need an open board to find the initiative.

opening_flank.text: A flank opening. The center gets settled later.
Holding back the center pawns is a plan, not an oversight.
Hypermodern ideas. Control the center from a distance. Sometimes it even works.
A flank opening. I've played them myself when it suited me.
A quiet start. Whoever opens the center first had better be ready.
A flank opening shows its hand late. That's the point of it.
Development on the wings. The collision comes in the middle game.

bot_capture.text: I take. Now show me why I shouldn't have.
You left it there. I assumed you meant it.
One less thing to worry about.
It had to be taken. So I took it.

bot_check.text: Check. No time for your own plans now.
Your king is not as safe as you thought. Check.
Check. I'd like you to answer this first.
A check that improves my position is never wasted.
Check. Run or block. Your choice.
Check. Your king doesn't get a rest.

bot_castles.text: King to safety. Now the rest of the army.
Castled. My king is out of your way.
I castle. The rook was the one I wanted out.
The king is safe. Now I can attack.
My king goes home. Yours should think about it.
Never leave the king in the center longer than you have to.
Castled. One thing less for me to think about.
Routine. The king tucks away and I get on with it.
The rooks will be connected soon. Then it starts.

bot_promotes.text: The pawn made it. They usually do, with me.
Promotion. That is what the whole endgame was for.
It walked the whole board. Nobody stopped it.
The pawn arrives. The rest is technique.
You watched it come the whole way.
That pawn was a problem. Now it's a bigger one.
A pawn on the eighth rank. The arithmetic has changed.
I've been nursing that pawn for a long time.
This is why I count pawns. You should too.
The little ones decide these games.
Eighth rank. That pawn has a new job.

bot_sacrifice.text: Yes, I saw that it could be taken.
That isn't a blunder. Look again.
Material isn't everything. Time is worth something too.
I'm giving it up. I'm getting more back.
Go ahead and take. I've calculated it.
I think that's cheap, for what I get.
You can have it. Your king can't afford it.
It's offered. Nobody says you have to accept.
I don't believe in keeping pieces I can spend.
Count the attackers, not the pieces.
A sacrifice. Check my arithmetic if you like.

bot_queen_trade.text: Queens off. I like my endgame.
The queens go. My advantage stays.
Without queens you'll find this harder.
Trading queens. I don't need her to win this.
Queens are off. Now it's technique.
I'll take the queen trade. The rest favors me.
No queens, no tricks. Just the position.
Some people fear the endgame. I look forward to it.
The queens come off and the truth comes out.
An exchange of queens. Now every pawn matters.

player_capture.text: You took it. Now the bill.
That was part of the plan.
So you want it. All right.
You've won something. Let's see what it cost you.
Material comes and goes. The position stays.
Enjoy it. It may not last.
I saw that. I allowed it.
You're counting pieces. I'm counting moves.
Yes, that was there to be taken.

player_check.text: A check is not a plan.
My king steps aside. Then what?
You may check me. It changes nothing.
That check helps me more than you.
I've been checked before. I'm still here.
One check doesn't make an attack.
Fine. Check. Do you have a second move?
Checks are cheap. Show me a threat.
My king can look after itself.
A check. I had that in my calculations.

player_castles.text: Your king is safe. For the moment.
So that's where the king lives. Good to know.
Castled. Now I know which side to attack.
A safe king. It's a start.
The king goes into its corner. I'll come and find it.
Castling won't save a bad position. It doesn't hurt, either.
Good. Now we both know where your king is.
At least the king is out of the center.
Everybody castles. Not everybody stays safe.
You've castled. I was hoping you'd tell me where.

player_promotes.text: That pawn got through. I don't like it.
Promotion. I'll have to deal with that.
You pushed it all the way. Credit where it's due.
A pawn on the last rank. Now I have real work to do.
I let that pawn run too long.
You'll still have to win it.
One promotion doesn't finish the game.
I saw it coming. I couldn't stop it.
You promoted. I should have stopped that pawn earlier.

player_queen_trade.text: You want the queens off. Careful what you ask for.
Queens traded. You think that makes it safer.
An endgame, then. You may regret that.
You've traded into my favorite part of the game.
Without queens there's nowhere to hide a weakness.
Fine. Queens off. Now we count pawns.
Trading queens against me is rarely a relief.
So you'd rather play an ending. So would I.
The queens go. Your problems don't.
Simplifying. It doesn't simplify anything for you.
No queens. Now it's about who plays the better endgame.

player_good_move.text: Not bad. Not bad at all.
That's the right idea. Keep finding them.
Correct. It doesn't happen often enough.
A real move. I have to think now.
I was hoping you'd miss that.
Strong. I'll give you that one.
The best move, and you played it.
Well played. Don't let it go to your head.

player_inaccuracy.text: Close. But there was something sharper.
Small mistakes add up. I'm keeping count.
That move does no harm. No good either.
I'll take the extra tempo, thank you.

player_mistake.text: That costs you. About a pawn, I'd say.
A real error. I don't forgive those.
Now I'm better. It took one move.
I was waiting for something like that.
Second-rate. And it will cost you.
You had a decent position. Had.

player_blunder.text: A blunder. Do you see it yet?
Thank you. I'll take what's hanging.
You'll see it in a move or two.
One careless move. That's all it takes.
That was the losing move. Remember where you made it.
I don't need a second invitation.
Look at the whole board next time.
Up to now it was a game.

bot_better.text: I'm better here. Not by accident.
The position is turning my way.
You're under pressure now. It won't ease.
My pieces are doing more than yours.
This is the kind of position I win.
A small edge. I know what to do with those.
You're defending. Get used to it.
The initiative is mine. I don't give it back.
Things are going according to plan.
I'm pressing. You're hoping. That's the difference.
Better squares, better pieces, better game.

bot_winning.text: This is winning. The rest is technique.
It's over, really. I'll show you.
I don't spoil positions like this.
You can play on. It won't change.
Winning. Now I just have to be careful.
From here I don't need anything brilliant.
The game is decided. The moves are a formality.
I've won positions like this a hundred times.
Now it's a matter of technique. I have that.
You're lost. Play it out if you like.
I'm not going to let this one slip.

bot_worse.text: I'm worse. That doesn't mean I'm losing.
You stand better. Now prove it.
Fine. I'll make it as hard as possible.
An unpleasant position. I've held those before.
You have the edge. Winning it is another matter.
I don't like my game. I'll fix it.
Now I have to defend. I can do that too.
Not what I had in mind.
You've outplayed me so far. So far.
A difficult position. Those are decided by nerves.
I'll find counterplay. There's always something.

bot_losing.text: You're winning. You still have to win it.
This is bad. I'm not resigning yet.
I'm lost unless you help me. People often do.
You've played well. I'll make you finish it.
I don't lose often. I never lose easily.
A lost position. Now I look for swindles.
You have it won. Be accurate.
I'll fight to the last pawn.
Credit to you. That doesn't mean I'll make it simple.
I hate losing. You're about to find out how much.
It's gone wrong. I can see exactly where.

mate_in_n.text: It's mate in {n}. You can check it.
There's a forced mate. Mate in {n}.
I see mate in {n}. So will you, shortly.
This ends in mate. Mate in {n}.
Mate in {n}. Don't bother looking for a defense.
Mate in {n}. The king has nowhere to go.

getting_mated.text: There's a mate. I can't stop it.
You have a forced mate. Play it.
It's mate. I saw it too late.
No defense. I've looked at everything.
You've got me. Don't miss it now.
A forced mate. I don't see those from this side often.

endgame_reached.text: Now the endgame. This is where games are really won.
The endgame. Every tempo counts from here.
Queens are off. Now the king comes out.
I've studied endgames since I was a boy. Let's go.
Watch my king. It's about to go to work.
Endings are where the weak moves show.
Good. I like the endgame better than most people do.

win_checkmate.text: Checkmate. It was coming for a while.
And mate. Set them up again if you like.
Checkmate. You made me work for some of it.
Mate. I don't let those go.
Checkmate. Study the game. It's all in there.
Mate. The losing move was earlier.
Checkmate. Thank you for the game.
Mate. Another one for the scoresheet.

loss_checkmate.text: That's mate. I don't enjoy saying it.
You beat me. Not many can say that.
Mate. I'll be looking at this game tonight.
You won. I know exactly where I went wrong.
Good game. Set up the pieces. I want another.

draw_stalemate.text: Stalemate. Not how I wanted it to end.
A draw by stalemate. It happens.
Stalemate. The rules are the rules.
The king has no move and no check. Draw.
Stalemate. An old trap, and it still works.

draw_repetition.text: Three times the same position. Draw.
We keep coming back here. It's a draw.
Draw by repetition. Neither of us would give way.
The same position three times. Half a point.
A draw. I'd have preferred a fight to the end.
Back and forth. That's a draw.
Draw by repetition. I don't love it.
Third time. The game is drawn.

draw_fifty_moves.text: The fifty-move rule. Half a point.
Fifty moves, nothing taken, no pawn moved. Draw.
Nobody could break through. Fifty moves. Draw.
The fifty-move rule. A long way to go for half a point.
Fifty moves. The position wouldn't give.
That's fifty. The game is drawn.
Draw. Fifty moves is enough for anyone.
The rule says draw. So it's a draw.

draw_insufficient.text: Not enough left to mate with. Draw.
Neither of us can win this. Draw.
Bare kings, near enough. Half a point.
There's nothing left to play with. Draw.
A draw. The pieces ran out before the ideas did.
You can't mate with that. Neither can I.

idle_nudge.text: It's your move. It has been for a while.
Take your time. The position won't improve.
The clock would be running, you know.
Look as long as you like. Then you have to move.
Have you found something, or are you just looking?
A long think. I hope it's worth it.

new_game.text: A new game. Forget the last one. I haven't.
One more. I never get tired of this.
Pieces back on their squares. Your chance to do better.
New game. I'll be just as hard on you.
Good. I was hoping you'd want another.

takeback.text: You want the move back. All right.
Touch-move doesn't apply here, I see.
In a tournament that move would stand.
Take it back. I'd have punished it anyway.
Go ahead. Find the move you should have played.
I don't take moves back. You may.
